title: Reading: 8-Bit and 16-Bit Hardware Still Being Built
content:
A link roundup, and a different kind of reading list. None of this is professional infrastructure advice, and I would not deploy any of it. It is here because the same engineering instincts apply to a machine with 64 KB of memory, and because the people building this stuff are doing careful, documented, verifiable work that is worth reading for its own sake.
The FPGA recreations. ZX Spectrum Next is the most ambitious: an FPGA implementation of a Z80 that stays compatible with the original while adding HDMI, WiFi and solid-state storage, and whose current issue adds licensed cores for the Sinclair QL and the Commodore 64. The interesting part is the compatibility constraint, which is the same problem as running a legacy workload and not breaking it.
MiSTer is the open-source answer, running dozens of machines on a Terasic DE10-Nano board. The community forum is where the real engineering happens, and it is very much alive.
MEGA65 is a real computer, not an emulator: a twenty-first-century realisation of the Commodore C65 that never shipped, running roughly forty times faster than a C64 while staying compatible. Real video chip, real keyboard, dual SD slots. Paul Gardner-Stephen has been at this for well over a decade and the documentation is exemplary.
Analogue Pocket takes a different approach, using two FPGAs for hardware-accurate recreation rather than emulation, and plays original Game Boy cartridges. Expensive, and opinionated about what faithful means.
Open hardware, cheap, and genuinely instructive. The Agon Light is an 8-bit machine and microcontroller in one, with an eZ80 and a BBC BASIC, at around fifty euros from Olimex. Neo6502 is a 6502 with an RP2040 coprocessor for thirty euros. CERBERUS 2100 has three CPUs and three CPLDs programmable down to individual gates, which is the one I would buy for teaching. And the ESP32-SBC at fifteen euros adds VGA and a keyboard to any microcontroller, which is the cheapest possible entry into writing an OS.
Operating systems, which is where I would start. FreeDOS is maintained, tested monthly, and the closest thing to a supported 16-bit DOS. AROS is API-compatible with AmigaOS without emulating it, the way Wine is to Windows. FreeMiNT is a multitasking kernel for the Atari ST. SymbOS is a preemptive graphical OS for Z80 machines and now runs on the Spectrum Next. KolibriOS is written in assembly, fits on a 1.44 MB floppy, and still ships a GUI, a browser and multitasking.
The reading, if you want the actual engineering. Leaded Solder is the best of these, covering hardware repair and bare-metal programming with real depth. Pagetable.com does C64 and 128 reverse engineering at a level that is genuinely difficult. The MiSTer wiki is where the FPGA architecture is explained properly, including the emulation versus replication distinction, which is the one that matters. RC2014 is a modular Z80 computer built from scratch with a monthly newsletter.
For reference material, Bitsavers has the manuals and schematics for essentially everything, and Vintage Computer Federation runs the events where the hardware actually gets shown.
Why this is on a site about infrastructure The constraints are what make it worth reading. Sixty-four kilobytes, no scheduler, no memory protection, and a bus you can count cycles on. Every abstraction we build on modern hardware has an equivalent here, expressed directly, and the design notes explain what it cost. The instinct that a system should be legible enough that you can hold it in your head is not modern, and reading about these machines is a good corrective for how much we assume it comes for free.
